Re analysis of diet protein study

The simulation study showed that a protein-identity distance goes blind when samples share no accessions, and that a TM-Vec ground metric does not. This report applies the same comparison to real data: 111 mouse faecal metaproteomes across eight dietary protein sources (Blakeley-Ruiz et al., ISME J 19(1) wraf048), quantified by spectral counting.

There is no weighted-UniFrac arm. The simulation could align 480 proteins from four families and give it a ground metric; here the universe is ~19,000 proteins from a whole gut community, mostly non-homologous, and there is no alignment to build a tree from.

Sys.setenv(KMP_DUPLICATE_LIB_OK = "TRUE")
reticulate::use_python(Sys.which("python3"), required = TRUE)

library(phyloseq)
library(vegan)
library(ggplot2)
library(gt)
library(here)
library(MicrobiomeStat)
for (f in list.files("R", full.names = TRUE)) source(f)

path  <- here("data", "test_study")
NPERM <- 9999

Data

ps <- readRDS(file.path(path, "ps.rds"))   # built and validated in data_curation.Rmd
ps
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 30561 taxa and 111 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 111 samples by 9 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 30561 taxa by 8 taxonomic ranks ]
## refseq()      AAStringSet:      [ 30561 reference sequences ]

Rarefaction

floor_depth <- min(sample_sums(ps))    # rarefy to the shallowest sample, dropping none

ggplot(data.frame(depth = sort(sample_sums(ps))), aes(seq_along(depth), depth)) +
  geom_col(width = 1) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = floor_depth, linetype = "dashed", color = "firebrick") +
  labs(x = "sample, sorted by depth", y = "PSMs") + theme_bw()

The shallowest samples sit within a few percent of each other, so there is no isolated outlier to drop and the cutoff (dashed line) is simply the minimum depth, 5760 PSMs. Taking it from min() rather than hardcoding it is what keeps that sentence true: any fixed number above the minimum silently discards the samples below it.

psd <- rarefy_even_depth(ps, sample.size = floor_depth, rngseed = 1,
                         replace = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)

# T0 has no protein source, so the diet term is undefined for it
psd <- prune_samples(sample_data(psd)$phase != "baseline", psd)
psd <- prune_taxa(taxa_sums(psd) > 0, psd)
sample_data(psd)$diet <- factor(sample_data(psd)$diet)
sample_data(psd)$dose <- factor(sample_data(psd)$dose)
psd
## phyloseq-class experiment-level object
## otu_table()   OTU Table:         [ 19192 taxa and 99 samples ]
## sample_data() Sample Data:       [ 99 samples by 9 sample variables ]
## tax_table()   Taxonomy Table:    [ 19192 taxa by 8 taxonomic ranks ]
## refseq()      AAStringSet:      [ 19192 reference sequences ]

Rarefying before pruning matters: rarefaction subsamples the raw counts, so it has to see the raw counts.

Embedding

TM-Vec1, the ground metric chosen in docs/ground_metric_models.md: its head was trained to regress the TM-score of protein pairs, so cosine similarity between two vectors is a predicted TM-score. Sequences are truncated at 1022 residues, TM-Vec1’s own limit from its ProtT5 encoder. The result is cached.

# cache = FALSE on purpose: this chunk's own code never changes, so knitr's
# chunk cache would not notice that `psd` changed upstream (e.g. a different
# rarefaction depth) and would silently replay a stale Z. The rds file below is
# the only cache, keyed by protein id, and it lives in data/ rather than in the
# knitr cache directory. Filename is model-specific (not "embeddings_tmvec.rds")
# so switching models can't silently reuse the previous model's vectors via the
# `need <- setdiff(...)` resume logic below.
cache <- file.path(path, "embeddings_tmvec1.rds")
Zall  <- if (file.exists(cache)) readRDS(cache) else NULL
need  <- setdiff(taxa_names(psd), rownames(Zall))

if (length(need)) {
  s <- substr(as.character(refseq(psd)[need]), 1, 1022)
  s <- s[order(nchar(s))]                       # length-sorted: keeps batches tight
  # Save every 2000 proteins rather than once at the end. The full pass is about
  # an hour and the cache is keyed by protein id, so an interrupted render resumes
  # from the last block instead of starting over.
  for (i in split(seq_along(s), ceiling(seq_along(s) / 2000))) {
    Zall <- rbind(Zall, embed_proteins(s[i], batch_size = 16))
    saveRDS(Zall, cache)
  }
}
Z <- Zall[taxa_names(psd), ]

Results

Bray-Curtis and Jaccard are both protein-identity distances – two proteins are either the same accession or maximally different – and differ only in whether abundance enters: Bray-Curtis weights by how much of each protein was detected, Jaccard only by whether it was detected at all.

cnt <- t(as(otu_table(psd), "matrix"))     # samples in rows
md  <- data.frame(sample_data(psd))
D <- list(`Bray-Curtis` = phyloseq::distance(psd, method = "bray"),
          `Jaccard`     = vegdist(cnt, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE),
          `weightedRep` = weightedRep(cnt, Z, method = "mmd"))

Amount of protein, sex and age stay in the model as covariates; only the diet term is reported. Permutations are blocked within mouse, since each mouse contributes several samples. sex is constant within a mouse, so it has no valid permutation distribution under that blocking — it absorbs variance rather than being tested.

diet_test <- function(dl) do.call(rbind, lapply(names(dl), function(n) {
  set.seed(1)
  a <- adonis2(dl[[n]] ~ diet + dose + sex + age_week, data = md, by = "terms",
               permutations = permute::how(blocks = factor(md$subject), nperm = NPERM))
  data.frame(distance = n, R2 = round(a["diet", "R2"], 3),
             F = round(a["diet", "F"], 2), p = a["diet", "Pr(>F)"])
}))
res <- diet_test(D)
r2  <- setNames(res$R2, res$distance)   # name-based lookup for the prose below
gt(res)
distance R2 F p
Bray-Curtis 0.281 9.60 1e-04
Jaccard 0.192 5.12 1e-04
weightedRep 0.335 11.80 1e-04
 
for (n in names(D)) {
  print(plot_ordination(psd, ordinate(psd, "PCoA", distance = D[[n]]), color = "diet") +
          stat_ellipse(type = "t", geom = "polygon", alpha = 0) +
          ggtitle(n) + theme_bw())
}

Diagnostics

A PERMANOVA \(p\) can come from groups differing in spread rather than in location, and the test cannot separate the two on its own. betadisper can.

gt(data.frame(
  distance     = names(D),
  betadisper_p = sapply(D, function(d) round(anova(betadisper(d, md$diet))$`Pr(>F)`[1], 4)),
  row.names = NULL))
distance betadisper_p
Bray-Curtis 0.0000
Jaccard 0.0000
weightedRep 0.5921

What Bray-Curtis and Jaccard are actually using

All three distances find a highly significant diet effect and land in the same broad range, which the simulation would not have predicted. The reason is that these are cage-housed lab mice searched against one protein database: samples really do share the same accessions, and exact accession identity is something Bray-Curtis and Jaccard can read directly. Jaccard’s lower \(R^2\) against Bray-Curtis’s is the presence/absence penalty: it throws away how much of each shared protein was detected, keeping only whether it was detected at all.

The test is to take that away. Give every sample its own private accession for each protein it detected. Counts, sequences and abundances are all unchanged — only the labels differ — so no two samples share an accession any more.

nz  <- which(cnt > 0, arr.ind = TRUE)
lab <- paste0("protein", seq_len(nrow(nz)))   # masked: one private label per (sample, protein) detection

cnt_s <- matrix(0L, nrow(cnt), length(lab), dimnames = list(rownames(cnt), lab))
cnt_s[cbind(nz[, "row"], seq_len(nrow(nz)))] <- cnt[nz]
Z_s <- Z[nz[, "col"], ]
rownames(Z_s) <- lab

c(accessions_before = ncol(cnt), accessions_after = ncol(cnt_s),
  max_samples_sharing_one = max(colSums(cnt_s > 0)))
##       accessions_before        accessions_after max_samples_sharing_one 
##                   19192                  125578                       1
res_s <- diet_test(list(`Bray-Curtis` = vegdist(cnt_s / rowSums(cnt_s), "bray"),
                        `Jaccard`     = vegdist(cnt_s, method = "jaccard", binary = TRUE),
                        `weightedRep` = weightedRep(cnt_s, Z_s, method = "mmd")))
gt(res_s)
distance R2 F p
Bray-Curtis 0.051 1.0 1e+00
Jaccard 0.051 1.0 1e+00
weightedRep 0.335 11.8 1e-04

Bray-Curtis and Jaccard both collapse to the exact null. Every pair is now maximally dissimilar, so each distance matrix is constant and cannot express any grouping: \(F = 1\), \(p = 1\), and \(R^2 = 5/98 = 0.051\), which is simply the diet term’s degrees of freedom over \(n-1\) — the share any 5-df term receives when there is nothing to explain. weightedRep() returns exactly what it returned above, because a protein’s embedding does not depend on what its accession is called and the abundance-weighted mean is therefore unchanged.

So Bray-Curtis’s and Jaccard’s whole result here rests on samples sharing literal accessions. That is a fair assumption within one colony, one database and one assembly. It stops being fair across studies, colonies or assemblies, where the same function arrives under a different accession — which is the case the representation distance is built for.

Differential abundance

PERMANOVA tests whether diet structures the community as a whole; it says nothing about which proteins carry that signal. Testing all 19192 proteins directly would mean that many near-independent tests on units that mostly aren’t independent – protein groups are frequently homologous (docs/method_notes.md §1), so a chunk of those “tests” are the same signal counted several times. rollupStructural() collapses proteins into bins where every member has predicted TM-score >= 0.5 to every other member – the same-fold threshold from Xu & Zhang (2010), already used above – before any testing happens, so multiplicity is paid once per structural unit, not once per accession.

roll <- rollupStructural(cnt, Z, cluster_threshold = 0.5)
c(proteins = ncol(cnt), bins = ncol(roll$counts))
## proteins     bins 
##    19192     1359

LinDA (Zhou et al., Genome Biology 2022) fits a linear model per bin on centered-log-ratio-transformed abundance and corrects the compositional bias a plain lm() on relative abundance would carry – the same reason weightedRep() works on abundance weights rather than raw proportions directly. Its formula interface takes a random effect for repeated sampling of the same mouse, the model-based counterpart to the permutation blocking adonis2 used above.

No prevalence filter – every one of the 1359 bins is tested, including the ones with only a handful of nonzero samples. LinDA warns about those rather than dropping them; the mixed model can also report a singular fit for a bin (its between-mouse variance estimated at zero), which lmer warns about but does not treat as an error.

fit <- linda(t(roll$counts), md,
            formula = "~ diet + dose + sex + age_week + (1 | subject)",
            feature.dat.type = "count", verbose = FALSE)
## Warning in linda(t(roll$counts), md, formula = "~ diet + dose + sex + age_week + (1 | subject)", : Some features have less than 3 nonzero values! 
##                      They have virtually no statistical power. You may consider filtering them in the analysis!

As with the PERMANOVA table, only the diet term is reported: a joint Wald test on all five diet coefficients per bin, LinDA’s counterpart to adonis2’s by = "terms".

L <- matrix(0, nrow = 5, ncol = length(fit$variables) + 1)
for (i in 1:5) L[i, i + 1] <- 1   # intercept + the 5 diet dummy columns
wald <- linda.wald.test(fit, L, model = "LMM", alpha = 0.05)
rownames(wald) <- rownames(fit$output[[1]])   # linda.wald.test drops them; reused below

gt(data.frame(bins_tested = nrow(wald), bins_diet_sig = sum(wald$reject),
              fraction_sig = round(mean(wald$reject), 3)))
bins_tested bins_diet_sig fraction_sig
1359 539 0.397

40% of bins reject at padj <= 0.05 – consistent with the PERMANOVA result above: diet is not a handful of marker proteins, it reorganizes abundance broadly across the structural repertoire. That joint test has no size to it, though – diet has five levels and no single number is “the” effect. A volcano plot needs one effect size per point, so the five diet-vs-Casein contrasts already inside fit are shown separately: one panel per diet, log2 fold change against Casein on the x-axis, each point one bin, red where that specific contrast rejects at padj <= 0.05.

diet_vars <- grep("^diet", fit$variables, value = TRUE)
volc <- do.call(rbind, lapply(diet_vars, function(v) {
  o <- fit$output[[v]]
  data.frame(bin = rownames(o), diet = sub("^diet", "", v),
             log2FoldChange = o$log2FoldChange, pvalue = o$pvalue, reject = o$reject)
}))

ggplot(volc, aes(log2FoldChange, -log10(pvalue), color = reject)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6, size = 1) +
  facet_wrap(~ diet, nrow = 1) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c(`FALSE` = "grey70", `TRUE` = "firebrick"), guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "log2 fold change vs Casein", y = expression(-log[10](p))) + theme_bw()

top <- volc[volc$reject, ]
top <- top[which.max(abs(top$log2FoldChange)), ]

members <- names(roll$bin)[roll$bin == top$bin]
t6 <- read.delim(file.path(path, "annotated", "ExtendedDataTable6AnnotatedMicrobialMetaproteomes.txt"),
                 skip = 2, quote = "\"", check.names = FALSE, colClasses = "character",
                 comment.char = "", fileEncoding = "latin1")
ann <- setNames(t6[["Consensus annotation"]], t6[["Protein Identifier"]])[members]
tx  <- as.data.frame(as(tax_table(psd), "matrix"))[members, c("Genus", "Species")]

The single largest shift, in either direction, is bin bin982 on Yeast: +7.3 log2 fold change against Casein at \(p=\) 7.7e-44. Its 16 members come from 2 different genera – proteins TM-Vec1 grouped as one predicted fold despite sharing no organism, the case an accession-identity distance cannot follow through a diet shift at all. Extended Data Table 6 annotates 2 of them, and every annotated one is a glycan-degrading enzyme – alpha-L-fucosidases and GH65/GH92 glycoside hydrolases, plausible machinery for a yeast-cell-wall-heavy diet, though this is one bin’s annotation coverage, not a pathway enrichment test.

info <- data.frame(
  Protein = members, Genus = tx$Genus, Species = tx$Species,
  `Annotation (Table 6)` = unname(ann),
  `Length (aa)` = Biostrings::width(refseq(psd)[members]),
  `Mean count, Casein` = round(colMeans(cnt[md$diet == "Casein", members, drop = FALSE]), 1),
  check.names = FALSE
)
info[[paste0("Mean count, ", top$diet)]] <-
  round(colMeans(cnt[md$diet == top$diet, members, drop = FALSE]), 1)
info <- info[order(-info[[ncol(info)]]), ]   # re-used below, so the sort has to stick
gt(info)

Every member sits at or near zero on Casein and climbs on Yeast, which is what the fold change states in raw counts – not an artifact of the log-ratio transform.

rollupStructural()’s complete-linkage guarantee is that every pair inside a bin has predicted TM-score >= cluster_threshold to every other member, not just to a nearest neighbor – true here by construction, but a heatmap shows what it looks like: the full pairwise predicted TM-score matrix for bin9, same protein order as the table above.

Zb <- Z[info$Protein, ]
S  <- 1 - as.matrix(proxy::dist(Zb, method = "cosine"))   # cosine == predicted TM-score
dimnames(S) <- list(info$Protein, info$Protein)           # kept protein-indexed, reused below

df <- as.data.frame(as.table(S))
names(df) <- c("i", "j", "TM_hat")
df$i <- factor(df$i, levels = info$Protein, labels = seq_along(info$Protein))
df$j <- factor(df$j, levels = info$Protein, labels = seq_along(info$Protein))

ggplot(df, aes(i, j, fill = TM_hat)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(0.5, 1), name = "predicted\nTM-score") +
  coord_fixed() +
  labs(x = "protein, table row above", y = "protein, table row above") +
  theme_minimal()

The floor is 0.81, comfortably above the 0.5 cutoff, and the diagonal is exactly 1 by construction (cos(z, z) = 1). The brighter blocks are sub-structure within the bin – proteins closer to a TM-score of 1 with each other than with the rest of the bin – but nothing drops below where complete linkage promised it wouldn’t.

Rows 1 and 2 stand out for a different reason: they are the two most abundant members of the whole bin, and also two of the ones with neither a Genus call nor a Table 6 annotation – invisible to a lineage-based method and to a profile-based one, grouped here on structure alone.

dark      <- info$Protein[is.na(info$Genus) & is.na(info[["Annotation (Table 6)"]])]
annotated <- info$Protein[!is.na(info[["Annotation (Table 6)"]])]

nn <- do.call(rbind, lapply(dark[1:2], function(p) {
  best <- annotated[which.max(S[p, annotated])]
  data.frame(Protein = p, `Predicted TM-score` = round(S[p, best], 3),
             `Nearest annotated neighbor` = best,
             Annotation = info[["Annotation (Table 6)"]][info$Protein == best],
             check.names = FALSE)
}))
gt(nn)
Protein Predicted TM-score Nearest annotated neighbor Annotation
BT_AB5-1_Cage1_bin.90_01179 0.950 AB21-1_Cage1_bin.62_00494 GH92 family glycosyl hydrolase
BT_AB5-1_Cage1_bin.90_01166 0.933 AB20-1_Cage1_bin.115_00129 GH92 family glycosyl hydrolase

Both of their nearest annotated relatives within the bin turn out to be the same protein: AB21-1_Cage1_bin.62_00494, a GH92 family glycosyl hydrolase from a different genus entirely – predicted TM-score 0.95 to BT_AB5-1_Cage1_bin.90_01179 and 0.933 to BT_AB5-1_Cage1_bin.90_01166. That is not a function call, just a specific, testable hypothesis where Table 6 offers none at all – exactly the gap a sequence-only annotation pipeline leaves open and a structural ground metric can speak to.

bin9’s two dark proteins are not a cherry-picked pair. Annotation-dependent tools – eggNOG-mapper, Pfam/HMMER, and whatever built Table 6’s “Consensus annotation” column here – only speak for a protein with a detectable match to something already characterized; the rest usually just drop out of any function-level discussion, not because they don’t matter, but because there is nothing to put in the annotation column. That gap is not rare here, and it is not concentrated in the boring part of the data:

is_dark <- function(ids) {
  a <- setNames(t6[["Consensus annotation"]], t6[["Protein Identifier"]])[ids]
  g <- as.data.frame(as(tax_table(psd), "matrix"))[ids, "Genus"]
  is.na(a) & is.na(g)
}
sig_members <- names(roll$bin)[roll$bin %in% rownames(wald)[wald$reject]]

gt(data.frame(
  scope    = c("whole protein universe", "diet-significant bins only"),
  proteins = c(ncol(cnt), length(sig_members)),
  dark     = c(sum(is_dark(colnames(cnt))), sum(is_dark(sig_members))),
  pct_dark = round(100 * c(mean(is_dark(colnames(cnt))), mean(is_dark(sig_members))), 1)
))
scope proteins dark pct_dark
whole protein universe 19192 1188 6.2
diet-significant bins only 12291 864 7.0

Proteins with neither a Genus call nor a Table 6 annotation are about as common among the proteins LinDA flagged as diet-associated as they are everywhere else in the dataset – being biologically important here (large fold change, high significance) bought them no better odds of being annotated. A structural ground metric does not fix the annotation gap, but it does not inherit it either: rollupStructural() places every protein in a bin whether or not it has a database hit, and a bin’s annotated members give its unannotated ones a specific, checkable neighbor instead of silence.

Conclusion

All three distances find dietary protein source highly significant, with diet \(R^2\) of 0.281 for Bray-Curtis, 0.192 for Jaccard, and 0.335 for the representation — the representation now reads more diet signal than Bray-Curtis, not just as much of it. The gain is real but not large, and the reason it exists at all is measurable: these samples share accessions, so protein identity, weighted or not, was already a good feature here.

Two more results separate the representation from the other two. Bray-Curtis fails the dispersion check while the representation passes, so part of the Bray-Curtis effect is diets differing in how variable they are rather than in where they sit. And once accession sharing is removed, both protein-identity distances drop to the null while the representation is untouched.

The honest reading is that the representation buys robustness and, here, a little power too. It keeps working where Bray-Curtis cannot — no shared accessions, no alignment, no tree, no annotation.

What this report does not settle is alpha diversity. Rarefying equalises depth, not evenness, and any abundance-weighted set distance can respond to how concentrated a sample is as well as to what is in it. Separating the two needs evenness matching or a support-corrected estimator, neither of which is done here.
